title: Glycemic index vs. glycemic load

seo.title: Glycemic index vs. glycemic load: the difference
seo.meta_description: GI describes carbohydrate quality; glycemic load adds how much available carbohydrate is in the serving. See the formula and practical examples.
seo.search_intent: Understand how glycemic index and glycemic load differ and when each is useful.

excerpt: Glycemic index (GI) describes the response to a standardized carbohydrate amount; glycemic load (GL) also accounts for how much available carbohydrate is in the serving you actually eat. GL = GI × grams of available carbohydrate per serving ÷ 100. A high-GI food can therefore have low GL when the serving contains little carbohydrate.
content_html:
Glycemic index and glycemic load answer different questions. GI describes the relative behavior of the carbohydrate; GL combines that behavior with the amount of carbohydrate in a real serving.

The formula is: GL = GI × grams of available carbohydrate in the serving ÷ 100.

The same GI can produce very different loads

Take a food with GI 70. A serving containing 40 g available carbohydrate has a GL of 28. A much smaller or more water-rich serving containing 6 g has a GL of only 4.2. The carbohydrate quality did not change; the dose did.

ExampleGIAvailable carbsGL
High-carbohydrate serving7040 g28
Low-carbohydrate serving706 g4.2

Why watermelon is the classic example

Watermelon can test relatively high on GI, yet a normal serving is mostly water and contains a modest amount of available carbohydrate. Its glycemic load can therefore remain low.

GL is not a complete nutrition score either

Low GL does not automatically mean nutrient-dense or minimally processed. GI and GL say nothing directly about protein, fat quality, vitamins, minerals or the overall pattern of the meal.

Glycemic load adds the amount you actually eat

Two foods can have a similar glycemic index yet produce very different glycemic loads when one normal serving contains far more available carbohydrate than the other. That is the point of the second concept: it puts absorption speed onto the scale of a real portion. Neither measure captures overall food quality on its own, because fiber, protein, fat, micronutrients and the rest of the meal still matter.

Which measure should you use?

Use GI to compare the intrinsic glycemic behavior of carbohydrate foods under standardized conditions. Use GL when portion size matters and you want a closer approximation of the carbohydrate impact of what you actually eat.

faq.question: How do you calculate glycemic load?
faq.answer: Multiply the food's GI by the grams of available carbohydrate in the serving, then divide by 100.

faq.question: Can a high-GI food have low glycemic load?
faq.answer: Yes. If a normal serving contains relatively little available carbohydrate, GL can be low even when GI is high.
